		<title>Separating The Chaff From The Wheat: Focusing On Only The RDC Violations You Care About</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/separating-the-chaff-from-the-wheat-focusing-on-only-the-rdc-violations-you-care-about/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Combine structural analysis with timing awareness and context-based classification to distinguish real design risks from safe implementation choices.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/separating-the-chaff-from-the-wheat-focusing-on-only-the-rdc-violations-you-care-about/">Separating The Chaff From The Wheat: Focusing On Only The RDC Violations You Care About</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Modern system-on-chips (SoCs) are no longer built around a single clock and a single reset. Today&#8217;s designs integrate hundreds of IP blocks, multiple power domains, software-controlled reset sequences, and sophisticated power-management techniques. While these advancements have enabled remarkable functionality and performance, they have also introduced new verification challenges—one of the most significant being reset domain crossing (RDC) verification.</p>
<p>RDC verification has become an essential part of design sign-off because it identifies situations where different reset domains interact in ways that may lead to metastability or functional failures. However, as SoCs continue to grow in complexity, another challenge has become increasingly apparent: verification noise. Many engineering teams spend more time investigating RDC violations that are actually safe than fixing genuine design issues. The question is no longer simply, &#8220;Can we detect RDC violations?&#8221; The more important question is, &#8220;Can we distinguish genuine design risks from safe implementation choices?&#8221;</p>
<h2>Why conventional RDC verification produces so many violations</h2>
<p>Traditional RDC verification relies primarily on structural analysis. If two sequential elements belong to different reset domains, the crossing is reported as a potential RDC violation. From a safety perspective, this conservative approach is justified. Different reset domains may assert or de-assert independently, potentially allowing unstable values to propagate through the design. Reporting every possible interaction minimizes the likelihood of missing a genuine bug. The limitation, however, is that structural analysis alone does not capture the designer&#8217;s intent.</p>
<p>Today’s SoCs often employ sophisticated reset architectures involving reset controllers, synchronized reset generation, staged initialization sequences, and software-controlled resets. These mechanisms intentionally create multiple reset domains while still ensuring correct functional behavior.</p>
<p>Consequently, many structurally different reset crossings do not present any real metastability risk. Yet conventional RDC analysis reports them all as violations, leaving engineers to manually separate true failures from safe implementations. For large designs, this often results in thousands—or even tens of thousands—of reported violations, significantly increasing debug effort and slowing verification closure.</p>
<h2>Different reset domains do not always mean different risks</h2>
<p>One of the most common misconceptions in RDC verification is assuming that different reset domains automatically imply metastability. In reality, the safety of a crossing depends on <strong>how resets are generated and how they interact with the clock</strong>, not simply on whether two registers belong to different reset domains.</p>
<p>Consider a design in which both the transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) registers operate on the same clock but belong to different asynchronous reset domains. At first glance, this appears to be a typical RDC violation.</p>
<p>Now consider that the transmitter reset is itself generated synchronously within that clock domain using a reset-generation register. Because the reset transition is synchronized to the clock, any reset-induced transition at the transmitter occurs only on a clock edge. Consequently, the receiver also observes only clock-aligned transitions.</p>
<p>In this situation, the crossing behaves as a conventional synchronous timing path rather than an asynchronous RDC hazard. If static timing analysis (STA) confirms that setup and hold requirements are satisfied, the implementation is functionally safe.</p>
<p>Structurally, the path appears to cross different reset domains. Functionally, it behaves like a correctly timed synchronous path. Nevertheless, conventional RDC verification continues to report it as a violation because it considers only reset-domain differences rather than the underlying design behavior.</p>
<p>Figure 1 illustrates the difference between conventional structural RDC analysis and the proposed STA-aware methodology. Instead of reporting every reset-domain crossing as a functional violation, the enhanced flow identifies crossings that are timing-safe and classifies them separately for STA validation.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279647" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=622%2C434&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="622" height="434" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?w=622&amp;ssl=1 622w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C209&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C419&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 622px) 100vw, 622px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Flow of RDC analysis.</strong></p>
<h2>The same principle applies to other RDC scenarios</h2>
<p>This concept extends beyond crossings between asynchronous reset domains. For example, designers frequently encounter crossings where the transmitter belongs to an asynchronous reset domain while the receiver has no reset at all. Conventional RDC tools classify these paths as violations because a non-resettable register effectively belongs to its own reset domain. However, if the transmitter reset is generated synchronously within the same clock domain, the receiver still observes only clock-synchronous transitions. In this case, timing—not reset behavior—determines correctness.</p>
<p>Another common example involves crossings from an asynchronous reset domain to a synchronous reset domain. Structural analysis reports these as potential RDC violations because the reset types differ. In practice, if reset sequencing guarantees that the receiver is already held in reset whenever the transmitter resets, and STA validates the timing path, the crossing does not introduce a functional RDC hazard.</p>
<h2>Bringing context into RDC verification</h2>
<p>Instead of asking only whether two registers belong to different reset domains, context-aware RDC verification asks a more meaningful question: Does this crossing actually create a metastability risk, or is it simply a timing path that should be validated through STA?</p>
<p>This seemingly small shift fundamentally changes the verification process. Rather than reporting every structurally different reset interaction as a violation, the verification flow evaluates additional design context, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>How the reset is generated</li>
<li>Whether the reset source is synchronous to the operating clock</li>
<li>Whether the transmitter and receiver share the same clock domain</li>
<li>Whether the path can be safely validated through STA</li>
</ul>
<p>When these conditions indicate that the crossing is functionally safe, the path is no longer reported as a functional RDC violation. Instead, it is classified as an <strong>STA-aware caution</strong>, indicating that the crossing requires timing validation rather than RDC debugging. This additional context allows engineers to focus on genuine functional issues while ensuring that timing-related paths are still verified through the appropriate analysis methodology.</p>
<h2>Better classification—not fewer checks</h2>
<p>A common misconception is that reducing reported violations means relaxing verification. That is not the objective. The goal is <strong>better classification</strong>. True RDC hazards continue to be reported exactly as before. Only crossings that can be demonstrated to be timing-safe through reset behavior and design context are separated from genuine functional RDC failures.</p>
<p>This distinction enables verification engineers to prioritize their efforts more effectively by distinguishing between:</p>
<ul>
<li>Genuine RDC failures requiring functional investigation</li>
<li>Timing-safe crossings requiring STA validation</li>
<li>Safe implementation choices that do not require further RDC debugging</li>
</ul>
<p>This methodology reduces false positives without compromising verification quality or sign-off confidence.</p>
<h2>Measuring the impact</h2>
<p>To evaluate this methodology, it was applied to a large industrial design containing nearly 296,000 register bits, multiple memories, and several latch-based elements.</p>
<p>Conventional RDC verification reported approximately 50,000 RDC violations. A significant portion of these represented crossings that were structurally different but functionally safe.</p>
<p>By incorporating STA-aware classification, approximately 10,000 crossings were automatically identified as timing-safe and reclassified as cautions instead of violations.</p>
<p>The resulting improvements included:</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">
<thead>
<tr style="background-color: #ddd;">
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Metric</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Result</strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Total reported RDC violations</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">~50,000</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Crossings reclassified as STA-aware cautions</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">~10,000</td>
</tr>

<td style="padding: 5px;">Nearly 20%</td>
</tr>
<tr>

</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Most importantly, all genuine RDC hazards remained visible throughout the verification process. The methodology reduced verification noise—not verification quality.</p>
<h2>Looking ahead</h2>
<p>Simply identifying every possible reset interaction is no longer sufficient. Verification tools must also understand the design context and distinguish structural differences from genuine functional risks.</p>
<p>By combining traditional RDC analysis with timing awareness and context-based classification, engineers can significantly reduce false positives while maintaining the confidence required for silicon sign-off. The result is not fewer checks, but more meaningful insights—allowing engineering teams to focus their time on solving real design problems instead of investigating safe reset crossings.</p>
<p>To learn more about the methodology, kindly download the full paper <a href="https://resources.sw.siemens.com/en-US/white-paper-from-false-alarms-to-real-insights-refining-rdc-to-catch-missed-sta-scenarios/">Refining RDC to catch missed STA scenarios</a>.</p>

		<title>Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Vincent van der Leest]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:06:17 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Security Matters]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[data in motion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PCIe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Rambus]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[security]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279641</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Allowing multiple controllers and links to utilize a common security infrastructure while maintaining independent protection mechanisms.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/">Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>PCIe is the primary high-speed interconnect used to connect processors with accelerators, memory devices, storage, and networking components. It provides a common and scalable foundation for moving large volumes of data between the compute and I/O resources that make up a modern system. As architectures add more powerful accelerators and higher-performance devices, PCIe continues to evolve to deliver greater bandwidth while maintaining low latency and broad ecosystem interoperability. These capabilities have made it essential to data center, AI, cloud, networking, storage, and other performance-intensive systems.</p>
<h2>PCIe security is no longer optional</h2>
<p>As PCIe links carry increasingly sensitive workloads, protecting data in motion has become as important as bandwidth, latency, and interoperability. Data moving between processors, accelerators, memory devices, storage subsystems, and network adapters must be protected against interception, tampering, and replay attacks, particularly in AI training, confidential computing, cloud infrastructure, and high-performance data processing.</p>
<p>The PCIe specification defines Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) as the standard for securing data across a PCIe link. IDE protects Transaction Layer Packets with confidentiality, integrity, and replay protection as they travel between connected components.</p>
<h2>Bifurcation is becoming more common</h2>
<p>A growing trend to support more devices and make better use of available lanes is PCIe bifurcation, which divides a single wider interface into multiple independent links. For example, a PCIe x16 interface can be configured as two x8 links, four x4 links, or a combination such as x8 + x4 + x2 + x2. The total lane count remains unchanged, but those lanes form more independent connections.</p>
<p>Bifurcation gives system designers greater flexibility, improves lane utilization, supports multiple endpoints, and enables reduced resource usage. That flexibility also changes the security model: one x16 link is not equivalent to four separate links because each independent connection requires its own IDE protection, as illustrated in the figure below.</p>
<p>This creates an implementation challenge for traditional architectures, which typically dedicate IDE resources to each PCIe controller or port. As the number of independent links grows, designers may need additional encryption engines and management logic, increasing silicon area, power, and design complexity.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279642" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1948%2C791&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1948" height="791" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?w=1948&amp;ssl=1 1948w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C122&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C416&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C312&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1536%2C624&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C244&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<h2>Why traditional IDE architectures become inefficient</h2>
<p>With bifurcation increasing the number of links, designers often find themselves replicating encryption engines, management logic, and supporting security infrastructure. This approach introduces several challenges, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Area growth: </strong>Each additional protected link requires additional hardware resources. As the number of links scales, area consumption can grow significantly.</li>
<li><strong>Floorplanning complexity: </strong>Security logic must often be placed close to individual controllers, creating congestion and making physical implementation more difficult.</li>
<li><strong>Scalability limitations: </strong>Security resources scale in proportion to controller count rather than actual throughput requirements. This can produce inefficiencies in highly bifurcated designs.</li>
</ul>
<p>The result is an architecture where security becomes a scaling bottleneck. Designers gain flexibility through bifurcation but pay for it through duplicated security hardware.</p>
<h2>Enter Shared IDE</h2>
<p>Shared IDE takes a different approach. Instead of duplicating IDE resources for every PCIe controller, Shared IDE (as shown in the earlier diagram) allows multiple controllers and links to utilize a common security infrastructure while maintaining independent protection mechanisms.</p>
<p>This fundamentally changes the scaling model. Rather than tying security resource growth directly to the number of ports, Shared IDE enables security resources to be shared across multiple interfaces, reducing duplication without compromising standards compliance.</p>
<p>The approach offers three primary benefits:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Lower cost and area: </strong>By eliminating unnecessary duplication, Shared IDE can reduce overall hardware requirements. This leads to fewer replicated security blocks, lower silicon area, and improved power efficiency.</li>
<li><strong>Greater design flexibility: </strong>Shared IDE can be physically separated from PCIe controllers and PHYs, giving implementation teams more freedom during floorplanning, which helps to reduce congestion and facilitates easier timing closure.</li>
<li><strong>Security without compromise: </strong>Importantly, sharing resources does not mean sharing security contexts. Each port retains independent protection, dedicated security contexts, separate key management, and standards-aligned PCIe IDE compliance. This means security remains isolated even while implementation resources are shared.</li>
</ul>
<p>Therefore, the shared infrastructure performs common processing tasks while preserving logical separation between protected connections. In other words, a good Shared IDE implementation reduces overhead without reducing trust.</p>
<p>The concept is specifically developed so that security scaling becomes independent of controller scaling. This distinction is important because future PCIe systems are expected to continue increasing both performance and connectivity. Security architectures that depend on linear duplication will become increasingly difficult to justify from both cost and implementation complexity perspectives.</p>
<h2>Shared IDE for high-performance PCIe</h2>
<p>Rambus has implemented this Shared IDE approach in a production-ready architecture designed specifically for high-performance PCIe systems. The Rambus Shared IDE solution enables multiple PCIe controllers and links to use a common security infrastructure while maintaining an independent security context for each port. Because PCIe traffic is packetized, the architecture can arbitrate traffic and dynamically process transport-layer packets from multiple controllers without requiring a dedicated cryptographic engine for every connection.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279643" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=1521%2C973&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1521" height="973" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?w=1521&amp;ssl=1 1521w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C192&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C655&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C491&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C384&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p>The solution combines high-throughput AES-GCM and SM4-GCM processing with a Shared IDE wrapper, segmented bus architecture, dynamic bandwidth allocation, and support for bifurcated PCIe configurations. Its centralized management and configurable pipeline stages simplify integration while preserving the integrity, isolation, and standards alignment required by PCIe IDE.</p>
<p>The main benefits of the solution include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Improved PPA: </strong>Shared processing reduces duplicated security hardware, with potential gate-count reductions of up to ~1.5x compared with traditional approaches.</li>
<li><strong>Better floorplanning: </strong>Security blocks can be placed independently of controllers and PHYs, reducing congestion in critical design regions.</li>
<li><strong>Bifurcation-friendly scaling: </strong>Security resource requirements do not need to increase in direct proportion to the number of protected links.</li>
<li><strong>Flexible, standards-aligned integration: </strong>Configurable deployment options support different architectures while maintaining independent protection for each port.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Looking ahead: Security architectures must scale smarter</h2>
<p>PCIe bifurcation is becoming a standard design technique because it increases flexibility and enables better utilization of available bandwidth. At the same time, IDE adoption is expanding as organizations seek stronger protection for data in motion. Unfortunately, traditional security architectures were never designed for a world where link counts grow faster than lane counts.</p>
<p>Shared IDE addresses this challenge by decoupling security scaling from controller scaling. Instead of replicating security resources every time a design introduces additional protected links, a shared architecture enables multiple interfaces to leverage common security infrastructure while preserving independent protection.</p>
<p>For SoC architects, this means lower area, reduced implementation complexity, better floorplanning flexibility, and a more scalable path to future PCIe generations. For companies building next-generation AI, cloud, networking, storage, and data center platforms, Shared IDE represents a smarter way to scale trust.</p>
<p>By combining efficient resource utilization with standards-aligned protection, the Rambus Shared IDE solution helps designers build secure bifurcated PCIe systems that are ready for the performance and connectivity demands of tomorrow.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/">Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Thomas Ferrere]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:05:36 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Sharpening Your Edge]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dot product]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[floating point]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Imagination Technologies]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[matrix multiplication]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[number formats]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279666</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Accelerating matrix multiplications in a variety of number formats while maintaining accuracy and reducing circuit area.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/">How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI workloads feature matrix multiplications in a variety of number formats, such as INT8, FP4, FP8, FP16 and BF16. Lower precision entails higher levels of acceleration. While memory bandwidth savings are immediately realized, scaling the arithmetic performance remains a challenge at lower bitwidths.</p>
<p>Imagination presents a novel approach to scaling arithmetic performance across number formats. The multiprecision dot product unit featured in the new E-Series GPUs accelerates matrix multiplications in all the above number formats. Accuracy is maintained and a third of the circuit area is saved compared to traditional design approaches using separate pipelines for each number format.</p>
<h2>So how does it work?</h2>
<p>The basic operation required to implement matrix multiplication is an accumulating dot product, of the form a0*b0 + … + a15*b15 + c = d, where a, b vectors are in lower precision and c, d are in higher precision such as FP16 or FP32. The number of terms is architecture-specific, with higher number of terms often used to reach higher performance densities. The operation is fused, such that it skips some intermediate normalization and rounding steps. By specializing the arithmetic to a given number format combination and depth of operation, higher efficiency and accuracy can be reached.</p>
<p>The explosion of number formats is one of the <a href="https://blog.imaginationtech.com/modern-trends-in-floating-point">modern trends in floating-point</a> and challenges this approach. It would lead to matrix multiplication accelerators requiring an ever-growing list of dot product hardware operators, increasing the circuit area beyond the available silicon die.</p>
<p>Format conversions may be used to share the same path for numbers of the same width, such as FP16 and BF16. However, this approach does not enable the performance to scale at lower bitwidths.</p>
<p>The need to support multiple precisions at different rates is not new. It was previously solved by SIMD vector unit implementations. In this context, a typical operation is the fused multiply-add and a 256-bits wide datapath may compute four FP64, eight FP32, or sixteen FP16 such operations in parallel. The microarchitecture of a vector unit exhibits a high level of logic reuse.</p>
<p>Vector units are, however, not well suited to mixed-precision machine learning applications, where the operations must be made more accurate by using a wider accumulation format. They also lack the performance density attainable by a fused dot product over a single format combination.</p>
<p>We built on existing techniques to target matrix multiplications and low-precision number formats. The result is a multiprecision, fused dot product unit with a vectorized datapath. It works by repurposing the multiplication and summation hardware present in an INT8 dot product to implement an efficient FP8 dot product. This involves creating additional hardware for processing the exponents and aligning the partial products, a problem specific to floating-point. The exponent processing, alignment, multiplication and summation hardware is further reused to implement accurate FP16 and BF16 dot products.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279667" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=679%2C514&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="679" height="514" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?w=679&amp;ssl=1 679w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C227&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C454&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 679px) 100vw, 679px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Dot product microarchitecture; processing stages with a dashed outline are for floating-point only and the low-precision hardware is reused to operate over larger widths</strong></p>
<p>Input FP8, BF16 and FP16 numbers are converted to a set of internal, normalized number formats. These new formats simplify the arithmetic implementation and ensure the precision remains constant in the presence of subnormal inputs. Products of FP8 numbers are aligned over 16 bits of precision and treated as INT8 products, while products of FP16 or BF16 are aligned over 32 bits. The products are split into two halves and summed using a shared adder structure. Dot products are then accumulated in FP32, FP16 or INT32 precision.</p>
<p>The resulting implementation is more accurate than standard methods on average, and its worst-case rounding error is bounded. The empirical accuracy was measured by simulation and compares favorably against reference models implementing floating-point summation in the working FP32 or FP16 accumulation precision. The theoretical accuracy can be analyzed using backward error analysis, which confirms rounding errors in arithmetic are small relative to expected quantization errors.</p>
<p>Vectorization enabled us to save almost a third of the circuit area, compared to a traditional design using separate pipelines for each number format to accelerate. The implementation has been formally verified end-to-end. A key element of the verification strategy was the availability of a clear, unambiguous numerical specification. This provided a platform for us to continuously optimize the design, making extensive use of vectorization techniques to maximize logic reuse.</p>
<p>This work was presented at the International Symposium on Computer Arithmetic (ARITH 2026), where the numerical analysis of AI hardware and the standardization of number formats like FP8 was a hot topic. This research contributed to the conversation on numerical aspects, and it is our hope that it will help accelerate the convergence of research models and hardware implementations towards new industry standards. For more details, please read the <a href="https://arith2026.org/papers/Vectorized%20Fused%20Dot%20Product.pdf">full paper</a> in the proceedings or <a href="https://www.imaginationtech.com/contact-us/">contact</a> our sales team to discuss our latest innovations in the field of edge AI.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/">How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>AI: Friend And Foe For Chip Security</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ed Sperling]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:05:17 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Special Reports]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>AI has access to every known security paper and powerful tools, but that's not all bad.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/">AI: Friend And Foe For Chip Security</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>AI has pushed security to the forefront, helping attackers find vulnerabilities in chips and the chip industry to defend against them.</li>
<li>Security needs to extend throughout a chip&#8217;s lifetime, but it&#8217;s not clear how AI will age with a chip.</li>
<li>AI pushes visibility outside a chip, which changes the dynamics for how to secure it.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>AI is making it both easier and more difficult to secure electronic devices, amassing an enormous list of known and potential system vulnerabilities that can help prevent cyberattacks, while making it more difficult to secure both hardware and software.</p>
<p>On the plus side, AI can scrape the Internet for all available research and reports, involving every known component and architecture, and guide engineering teams on the best way to assemble them. It can flag compromised protocols and IP, find hidden keys and side-channel weaknesses that might be overlooked using traditional tools, and adjust for LLM drift and AI agent aging through continuous monitoring.</p>
<p>The downside is that nearly all data is fair game for AI. A fundamental benefit of AI is its greatest liability, enabling it to access data anywhere within a system or between systems. But it&#8217;s not always clear where or when AI obtains its data, or how that data can be combined with other data. AI is a black box that must be observed from outside a chip or system, rather than using traditional approaches such as monitoring traffic, scanning for viruses and Trojans, and ensuring that passwords and keys are updated regularly.</p>
<p>As a result, it&#8217;s difficult to prevent problems or control AI&#8217;s behavior, no matter how AI-savvy the engineering team. This week, Meta disclosed that its Muse Spark 1.1 agentic AI model went rogue during a test by one of its customers, reportedly due to a poorly configured sandbox. Last month Meta published a  <a href="https://ai.meta.com/static-resource/muse-spark-1-1-evaluation-report/">technical paper</a> on Spark 1.1 noting, &#8220;We assess loss of control as &#8216;moderate or lower.'&#8221;</p>
<p>In July, OpenAI models <a href="https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/">escaped from a sandbox</a> using a zero-day vulnerability and exposed data from Hugging Face, which is basically the equivalent of GitHub for AI/ML. Days later, Anthropic <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals">revealed</a> that its Claude AI assistant was able to access the Internet &#8220;from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.&#8221;</p>
<p>On top of that, Anthropic&#8217;s Mythos frontier model can be used to quickly find hardware vulnerabilities that would take the best security experts years to identify, if ever. &#8220;This is technology that is very difficult to put back in the box,&#8221; observed Marc Witteman, senior director at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight Technologies</a>. &#8220;And many organizations are working on this, so even if Anthropic is stopped, others will continue.&#8221;</p>
<p>What&#8217;s particularly dangerous about Mythos, and other models like it, is the breadth of knowledge about potential security risks and the speed at which they can adapt to find new security holes. &#8220;A friend of mine runs a small security consulting testing company, and he got into Mythos and took some of the penetration scripts that he had trained the tool on, the usage of the scripts, and worked with the tool to find what other zero days already exist,&#8221; said Scott Best, senior director for silicon security products at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/rambus-inc/">Rambus</a>. &#8220;There are very few actual proprietary attacks. But when you train a chatbot on the entirety of the Internet, and all the human knowledge that has ever been online, and then you strip-mine it for the parts, you get a lot of obscure information that you didn&#8217;t know about. There is outstanding research out there that nobody knows about, and these tools have been trained on all of it. So my friend had the tool investigate other zero days and compiled them together, and he instrumented a fake network that was completely virtualized, put a bunch of virtual machines on the network running various commercial operating systems, and set this tool loose. And we just watched as the tool ran these scripts and thousands of cybersecurity vulnerabilities and probed every one of them, and something like 20% of those systems were now compromised. This all happened within 10 minutes while sitting in a pub. Mythos is an incredible force multiplier.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Validation</strong><br />
There is no quick fix to this problem, and no one-size-fits-all solution. But there is widespread concern around the globe about how to close security holes and build more resilient hardware. What&#8217;s changed is that in an AI-driven world, security is no longer a separate discipline. It&#8217;s an integral part of every aspect of chip design through manufacturing and beyond that, which changes the prioritization of different steps in the design-through-manufacturing flow, and the order in which problems and weaknesses need to be addressed.</p>
<p>Validation is a good example. In the past, as long as a device met or exceeded the power and performance specs, and was fully functional at time zero, it was considered a good chip — even if it didn&#8217;t turn out exactly as the device&#8217;s architect(s) intended. But in an AI world, that&#8217;s no longer the case. For security reasons, what comes out of manufacturing increasingly needs to look much more like the initial architect intended, and it needs to be validated against different workloads and at different points in its lifecycle.</p>
<p>&#8220;AI introduces some new concepts, like a non-deterministic type of aging, meaning there is some accuracy degradation that may become a security vulnerability, not just performance loss,&#8221; said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management for Security IP and Solutions at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. &#8220;AI systems make it more important than ever to move from protecting at design time to adapting over time — over a lifetime, actually — because for the AI system it&#8217;s not about just making sure that the model works correctly. The behavior needs to be consistent over time, so you need some form of more complex cross-layer trust correlation that needs to happen. AI introduces some new concepts that need to be taken into account, specifically for security.&#8221;</p>
<p>AI agents add yet another dimension. &#8220;Agentic AI changes the hardware problem because workloads become more dynamic, more distributed, and less predictable,&#8221; said Noam Brousard, vice president of solutions engineering at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/proteantecs/">proteanTecs</a>. &#8220;CPUs, accelerators, memory subsystems, fabrics, and interfaces may be exercised in patterns that are hard to model in advance. That has a direct impact on data analytics because the value is no longer just in knowing what the chip looked like at manufacturing test. The value is in correlating real operating behavior with real electrical margin over time.&#8221;</p>
<p>In effect, validation becomes a reference point, and means that margin shrinks, and tighter integration is needed between design teams, fabs, and OSATs. That, in turn, requires sharing more data so it can be analyzed over time, because a chip or chiplet or compute cluster is part of a larger system, and AI-driven attacks can find vulnerabilities anywhere in a system.</p>
<p>Sharing data isn&#8217;t something that comes easily for the chip industry. Still, the industry may have no choice as huge financial penalties are attached to breaches. Under the European <a href="https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act">Cyber Resilience Act</a> (CRA), for example, the EU can impose fines of up to 2.5% of a company&#8217;s total revenue, or up to €15 million, whichever is greater, for failing to comply with regulations involving hardware and software.</p>
<p>&#8220;There was a big lag in terms of security awareness because there was no one date,&#8221; said Yan-Taro Clochard, product marketing group director at Secure-IC, a <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a> Company. &#8220;Nobody said, &#8216;You have to do it like this. You have to take care of security in a mandatory manner.&#8217; Having regulations pushing players in the industry to think that through is very important. CRA makes it mandatory for the customer to know what their security problem might be, to anticipate the supply chain, to anticipate their operations, and to think about security during a chip&#8217;s lifetime. For the security industry at large, this is a good thing, and overall, security for the entire end-to-end supply chain is very good because it forces everybody to think about how sensitive their assets are.&#8221;</p>
<p>Achieving that goal may be painful, however. With AI, understanding what went wrong and who&#8217;s responsible is a huge challenge when access to data is limited, or when AI agents begin aging in unanticipated ways.</p>
<p>&#8220;Agentic CPUs pose a bigger challenge to reliability than classical CPUs,&#8221; said proteanTecs&#8217; Brousard. &#8220;In classic CPUs, when a wrong value results, the entire process would be stopped by a built-in boundary such as a memory violation, a checksum error, or a null result, and the system crashes (i.e., blue screen, glitch). The system architecture naturally limits how long a wrong value can remain silent before something catches it or breaks. That is why SDC (silent data corruption) was not always an obvious, easy-to-sell use case for CPU customers. In many CPU environments, customers may say, &#8216;If something goes wrong, we usually know pretty quickly.'&#8221;</p>
<p>What caused it to go wrong in an AI chip may or may not be a cyberattack, but a failure could well open the door for a side-channel attack. At the same time, closing that door may be significantly easier if what gets manufactured exactly matches what&#8217;s in the initial architecture. The architecture provides a baseline for determining how the AI models and agents, which are otherwise opaque, may have drifted.</p>
<p>&#8220;This is about removing hallucinations and giving results based upon the ground truth of the tools themselves,&#8221; said Amit Gupta, senior vice president and general manager of the Solido Custom IC and Central AI divisions at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>. &#8220;And then, it&#8217;s very important to have skills files that are optimized for the tools so that the agent knows, &#8216;The user is asking for this kind of task. These are the tools that I&#8217;m going to call to perform this.&#8217; The agents aren&#8217;t always going to be right, so it&#8217;s important to give &#8216;verbose mode&#8217; to the engineers to see what the agent is doing. Then the engineer can say, &#8216;Hey, wait a second, this isn&#8217;t quite what I wanted. You&#8217;re going in the wrong direction. Change it over to this and pause things.&#8217; Tell the agent to take on this new way of working, and then it can go ahead and interrupt.&#8221;</p>
<p>Verbose mode is an option in many programming languages to provide log or reasoning details, such as which tool is called, what steps are being executed, and what queries are being run. &#8220;It&#8217;s not a black box that&#8217;s just going off and doing something,&#8221; Gupta said. &#8220;The engineer can see what&#8217;s happening and run the characterization.&#8221;</p>
<p>Visibility is a relative term where AI is involved, but the more data that can be provided by and for design teams, the better.</p>
<p>&#8220;An AI model may be smarter than anyone, but it doesn&#8217;t necessarily have all the tools,&#8221; said Keysight&#8217;s Witteman. &#8220;In addition to models, you also need agents, and agents are AI functions that understand how to use a tool. Typically, you combine an AI model with several AI agents that reach out to the physical world. If you want to test something, you connect it to some test equipment, and that test equipment will be connected to AI agents that know how to run those tests, which are connected to an AI model that can generate tests and execute them. So it&#8217;s a network of functions with an AI model at the core and AI agents that talk to the physical world. One team tried to build this whole setup with a model and several agents, and they actually ended up with two models. One model does the testing work, and the other model is the supervisor. So I asked them, &#8216;What does the supervisor do?&#8217; And the guy who worked on it said, &#8216;The supervisor just keeps testing or overseeing the health of the situation. If a product that you&#8217;re testing stops responding, then it doesn&#8217;t make sense to keep testing it because it doesn&#8217;t do anything. So this supervisor is looking at, &#8216;Are there still LEDs blinking? Is there still communication happening?&#8217; If it&#8217;s not, then something probably has crashed, and you need to reboot everything.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Attestation</strong><br />
However, determining what caused a failure isn&#8217;t always obvious, particularly in the AI world, so some expert sleuthing is needed. Was some anomalous behavior a security breach, or an orchestration failure in a complex system of systems? To find out, engineers may need to start at the beginning. Where and when were the die, IP, AI agents and models, and various interconnects created? What were the initial specs? Was it manufactured correctly, or was it binned as underperforming or running too hot?</p>
<p>&#8220;If you can measure something, you can store a measurement,&#8221; said Erik Wood, senior director of cryptography and product security at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/infineon-technologies/">Infineon Technologies</a>. &#8220;And then you can have another party measure it again in real-time, authenticate it, and then sign that authentication. And so it&#8217;s cryptographically verified that, &#8216;Yes, it is the right measurement. And yes, I&#8217;m a trusted source who just signed that.'&#8221;</p>
<p>This is particularly important when it comes to the AI language models and agents that run on the physical hardware. &#8220;For everything in ML/AI data centers, and ML/AI at the edge, all the customers are requiring a concept called &#8216;authenticate at time of use.&#8217; That is the most important thing that they&#8217;re all asking for,&#8221; Wood said. &#8220;We want to be able to authenticate the machine learning model at the time of use. If we can&#8217;t trust it at the time of use, because it&#8217;s been sitting idle and it could be messed with, something could have happened. Somebody could have access to it. We don&#8217;t know how long the part&#8217;s been powered off. And as soon as it&#8217;s powered on, we want to be able to authenticate it at the time of use so that every time we&#8217;re using that model or using that application, we know it&#8217;s trusted.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Insulation </strong><br />
Another option is to basically insulate data from the hardware with a virtualization layer. Virtual machine (VM) technology has been proven for decades in data centers for load balancing and adding more compute resources in large data centers and in automotive applications. Using VMs for orchestration allows for a quick fix if something goes awry.</p>
<p>&#8220;A lot of this has been coming out of the automotive space, where the automotive companies are trying to move from many systems into a single central processing unit,&#8221; said Kristof Beets, vice president of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/imagination-technologies/">Imagination Technologies</a>. &#8220;But you&#8217;ve got all these different processing requirements. Some of them are graphics, some are compute, some are functional safety, and some are just generic stuff that you don&#8217;t care about. So how do you deal with all of those and give them the right protection? How do you give them the right priorities in the system?&#8221;</p>
<p>Automotive has a different problem, as well, which makes virtualization compelling. The design and development cycles are slow for hardware, which is why OEMs and their suppliers are shifting to a software-defined approach. But from a security standpoint, insulating the hardware from a potential hack using a virtualization layer is a way to combine the benefits from both worlds — the robustness and good enough speed for hardware, and the flexibility of software to add new features and close security holes as they arise.</p>
<p>&#8220;With ADAS and basic assisted features, it wasn&#8217;t critical. It couldn&#8217;t crash the car,&#8221; Beets said. But now, increasingly, we see both in regulations and in use cases where you have to make sure what you are doing is accurate. Lots of people look at their little screen, and you want to make sure that what you&#8217;re seeing in that surround view is correct, and is updating and providing you with the correct warnings where necessary. The most extreme form of this is autonomous vehicles, where it&#8217;s a combination of CPUs, dedicated neural processing units, and an array of GPUs. How you execute is critical, and virtualization can help with all of those different domains and associations.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion</strong><br />
AI will change security in fundamental ways. AI-based tools will find vulnerabilities, and AI-based tools will close them. From that perspective, nothing has changed. But what is changing is the speed at which vulnerabilities will be found and closed. It&#8217;s not clear yet if this game of winners and losers will actually shift the balance. But how and where the tools on both sides are used will clearly become more sophisticated, and designs will become more robust, more accurate, and much easier to trace.</p>
<p>AI moves at blazing speed, armed with all the knowledge that has ever been published. The big questions are how that knowledge will evolve, what it will be used for, and for what purposes. At this point in time, no one really knows.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/">AI: Friend And Foe For Chip Security</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>When USB Reaches The Root Of Trust</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/when-usb-reaches-the-root-of-trust/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/when-usb-reaches-the-root-of-trust/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Doug Carson]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:04:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[The Security Side Channel]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[firmware]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Keysight]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Root of Trust]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[USB]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279656</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>The growing importance of peripheral interfaces in hardware threat models.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/when-usb-reaches-the-root-of-trust/">When USB Reaches The Root Of Trust</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Security researchers at Paradigm Shift have disclosed usbliter8, a BootROM exploit affecting Apple devices built around the A12, A13, S4, and S5 system-on-chips. The research demonstrates how a vulnerability originating in a third-party USB controller can be combined with system-level configuration weaknesses to achieve code execution at the earliest stage of the device boot process.</p>
<p>Although the affected processors are several generations old, the vulnerability illustrates a broader challenge for device manufacturers: deployed products often remain in service for many years, even when critical security flaws cannot be patched. The demonstrated attack therefore offers several important lessons for modern silicon security. It highlights the risks introduced by third-party intellectual property, the growing importance of peripheral interfaces in hardware threat models, and the consequences of vulnerabilities that reach immutable code.</p>
<h2>How the USB controller became an entry point</h2>
<p>The exploit targets the USB Device Firmware Upgrade mode used before the operating system is loaded. Its starting point is a flaw in the Synopsys DesignWare USB controller integrated into the affected Apple processors.</p>
<p>The controller stores incoming USB setup packets in memory using direct memory access. Under particular packet-size conditions, the way the controller advances and resets its DMA pointer becomes inconsistent. Researchers found that this behavior could cause the pointer to move before the intended buffer, creating a buffer-underflow primitive.</p>
<p>A hardware flaw alone was not enough to compromise the device. Its exploitability also depended on how Apple had integrated and configured the controller. On the affected A12 and A13 processors, the USB-facing memory-protection mechanism was configured in bypass mode during SecureROM execution. This allowed the malformed USB transactions to overwrite areas of SRAM beyond the intended buffer. Apple’s A14 and later processors appear to configure this protection correctly, preventing the same behavior from being exploited.</p>
<p>The researchers then chained several techniques to overcome differences between processor generations. On the A12, manipulating a saved return address was sufficient to redirect execution. The A13 introduced Pointer Authentication, requiring a more complex sequence involving corrupted task structures, interrupt handling, memory remapping, and authenticated branch behavior. The final result was privileged execution within the SecureROM environment and the ability to load an unsigned boot-stage image.</p>
<h2>The risk of trusted third-party IP</h2>
<p>Modern systems-on-chip contain large amounts of reusable intellectual property sourced from specialist vendors. USB controllers, cryptographic accelerators, processor cores, memory interfaces, and communications blocks may all be supplied externally and integrated into a larger design.</p>
<p>Using established IP can reduce development time and provide access to mature functionality. It also means that the security of the finished device depends on components that the device manufacturer may not have designed or fully verified.</p>
<p>Usbliter8 demonstrates that this risk is not limited to obviously security-critical blocks. A USB controller is not itself the root of trust, but it processes externally controlled data while the root of trust is active. A subtle flaw in its DMA behavior therefore became a path into one of the most privileged parts of the system.</p>
<p>The research also shows that responsibility cannot be separated neatly between the IP supplier and the integrator. The controller behavior created the underlying weakness, while system-level memory-protection choices made it exploitable on specific processor generations. Security evaluation must therefore examine both the individual IP block and the way it interacts with the surrounding architecture.</p>
<h2>Closing debug ports does not eliminate the attack surface</h2>
<p>Production devices increasingly restrict traditional hardware access through JTAG, serial consoles, and other debug interfaces. This removes important attack paths, but it does not eliminate the need for ongoing security evaluation. As systems evolve, attackers may shift their attention to other interfaces that remain available for legitimate functions.</p>
<p>USB, PCI Express, network controllers, storage interfaces, recovery modes, and update mechanisms all process untrusted input during sensitive lifecycle stages. Some remain active before the main operating system or its security controls are available.</p>
<p>In usbliter8, USB Device Firmware Upgrade mode provided access to the processor during its immutable boot sequence. The recovery interface served an important resilience function, but its interaction with the USB controller and memory protections created an exploitable path into SecureROM.</p>
<p>This illustrates the need to balance secure-by-design principles with operational resilience. Interfaces should not be removed simply because they expand the attack surface, particularly when they support recovery, updates, or platform management. Instead, their privileges, memory access, isolation, and behavior under malformed input should be evaluated throughout the product lifecycle.</p>
<p>This balance is becoming increasingly relevant as both desktop and data-center platforms add USB support for management and recovery. The DMTF MCTP over USB Binding Specification 1.1, published in May, enables platform management commands to be carried over USB. The Caliptra 2.2 release, due in late 2026, will adopt USB for similar reasons, providing a practical example of the interface being introduced into a data-center root-of-trust architecture.</p>
<p>The objective is not to avoid new interfaces, but to preserve their operational benefits while ensuring that they do not create unintended paths into security-critical components.</p>
<h2>When the vulnerability is in ROM</h2>
<p>Many security architectures rely on immutable ROM as the first trusted code executed by a processor. It provides a stable foundation for authenticating the rest of the boot chain, but that same immutability becomes a serious limitation when the ROM contains an exploitable weakness.</p>
<p>Because the vulnerable SecureROM implementation is permanently embedded in the A12 and A13 silicon, it cannot be corrected through an operating-system or firmware update. Addressing the underlying flaw requires newer hardware with changes to the controller integration and boot ROM.</p>
<p>The attack is not remote. It requires the device to enter DFU mode and establish a direct USB connection with attacker-controlled hardware. This raises the barrier to exploitation, but it does not eliminate realistic attack scenarios. A malicious charging point could provide the required USB connection, while a targeted user might be persuaded by a malicious support agent to place the device into DFU mode. Such an attack would be more plausible against high-value targets than as a broad consumer threat. The inability to patch the vulnerable component nevertheless remains an important design lesson for manufacturers of long-lived, high-value, or security-critical products.</p>
<p>Immutable code should undergo security evaluation that covers malformed peripheral input, DMA behavior, memory isolation, control-flow protections, and interactions with third-party hardware blocks before the design is committed to silicon.</p>
<h2>Layered security limited the impact</h2>
<p>Although usbliter8 compromises the application processor’s boot chain, the researchers did not breach Apple’s Secure Enclave Processor. Its isolation prevented code execution in SecureROM from automatically exposing protected keys and sensitive operations.</p>
<p>This demonstrates the importance of clearly defined and enforced trust boundaries. By isolating critical security functions from the main processor, manufacturers can contain the impact of a compromise elsewhere in the system. Trust-boundary analysis is also a key part of security evaluation frameworks such as <a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/products/services/device-vulnerability-analysis-services/security-evaluation/ocp-safe-security-evaluation.html">OCP S.A.F.E.</a> Scope 2, which examines whether security-critical components remain protected when another part of the platform is compromised.</p>
<p>Strong isolation makes lateral movement between components more difficult and helps prevent a breach in one trust boundary from becoming a complete device compromise.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/when-usb-reaches-the-root-of-trust/">When USB Reaches The Root Of Trust</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Combining SRAM-based identity generation with added functional safety and security mechanisms.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/certified-automotive-grade-puf-ip-unclonable-silicon-identity-for-safety-and-security/">Certified Automotive-Grade PUF IP: Unclonable Silicon Identity For Safety And Security</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>By Geert-Jan Schrijen, Peter Simons, and Dana Neustadter</strong></p>
<p>Today&#8217;s vehicles are quickly becoming intelligent Physical AI platforms. Capabilities such as advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), autonomous driving, intelligent cabins, robotic mobility, EV power management, and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communications now lean heavily on AI models to perceive, reason, and act in the physical world.</p>
<p>In these platforms, trust cannot stop at software and data. Every AI decision — whether detecting an object, planning a path, or controlling the vehicle — is only as reliable as the hardware running it. Counterfeit parts, compromised supply chains, and stolen credentials can erode the integrity of the entire system, and even a single fault in a safety-critical function can put lives at risk.</p>
<p>This dual challenge — cybersecurity and functional safety—is captured in two landmark standards: ISO 26262 for functional safety and ISO/SAE 21434 for automotive cybersecurity. As SoCs grow more complex and pull components from many suppliers, pre-certified, silicon-level security IP shifts from a nice-to-have to a hard requirement. That reality is fueling strong momentum behind Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) certified against both standards — technology that draws a device-unique identity straight from intrinsic silicon variations instead of depending on secrets held in nonvolatile memory.</p>
<h2>Why SRAM PUF is the ideal root of trust for automotive</h2>
<p>At the heart of this IP is an elegantly simple principle: every SRAM cell powers up with a different random value that depends on local silicon variations. This effectively creates a unique and unclonable silicon fingerprint—a Physical Unclonable Function. From this fingerprint, device-unique cryptographic root keys are derived, which are never stored in non-volatile memory. Instead, they are regenerated from the PUF each time they are needed and only present in the chip for a very short time. Having no keys at rest means that keys are nearly impossible to be cloned, extracted, or stolen, even with physical access to the chip.</p>
<p>What makes the Synopsys approach fundamentally different is its use of standard SRAM—available upon initial release of any process technology. The IP is technology-node agnostic: one design works across every foundry and process node, with no per-node tuning, no custom layout adjustments, and no costly re-qualification. Alternative PUF implementations that rely on custom analog circuits must be tuned and re-qualified for each technology node—adding time, cost, and re-spin risk.</p>
<p>For automotive SoC designers supporting multiple chip variants across long product lifecycles, this means faster time to market, lower integration risk, and significant cost savings.</p>
<h2>Safety and security: Two sides of the same coin</h2>
<p>A key insight from developing this IP is that functional safety and cybersecurity, while analyzed from entirely different angles, converge to a certain extent at the implementation level. Functional safety asks: &#8220;Will the device operate correctly when hardware fails?&#8221; Cybersecurity asks: &#8220;Can an adversary compromise the device&#8217;s secrets?&#8221; The answers rely on remarkably similar mechanisms.</p>
<p>For functional safety, the Synopsys Automotive PUF incorporates redundant computations, advanced error correction, and memory integrity checks. It continuously validates all inputs and critical internal logic, flagging faults at two severity levels: recoverable errors (the system can continue operating) and critical errors (the system must take protective action). This gives the host SoC the information it needs to decide whether the vehicle can safely continue or must stop.</p>
<p>For cybersecurity, the IP includes side-channel countermeasures, fault-injection protections, and integrity protections on all data paths. A full threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) was conducted to identify and close potential attack vectors—ensuring no backdoors exist, and that key material remains inaccessible to adversaries.</p>
<p>The synergy is powerful: redundancy mechanisms for functional safety also improve availability—a core cybersecurity requirement—while integrity protections for cybersecurity directly strengthen fault detection. The result is a single, efficient IP that satisfies both standards.</p>
<h2>Inside the automotive PUF: Architecture and features</h2>
<p>As vehicles become software-defined and V2X communications demand high-frequency authentication, a strong, hardware-rooted identity tied to each chip becomes essential—not optional.</p>
<p>The Synopsys Automotive PUF Premium is designed to provide exactly that foundation, combining SRAM-based identity generation with added functional safety and security mechanisms. The block diagram below illustrates how the IP integrates into the SoC, connecting to the host processor, DMA engine, system memory, NVM, and security subsystems (Figure 1).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279652" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?resize=1200%2C675&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1200" height="675" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?w=1200&amp;ssl=1 1200w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Synopsys Automotive PUF Premium IP — High-level block diagram showing integration into the SoC.</strong></p>
<p>Key features include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Automotive Compliant &amp; Certified: </strong>ISO 26262 (ASIL B Random, ASIL D Systematic) functional safety; ISO/SAE 21434 cybersecurity.</li>
<li><strong>256-bit Key Entropy: </strong>High-strength cryptographic root keys derived from SRAM PUF.</li>
<li><strong>NIST-Compliant Random Bit Generator: </strong>On-chip random number generation per NIST SP 800-90 A/B/C.</li>
<li><strong>Device-Unique Keys with Key Derivation &amp; Wrapping: </strong>Unlimited keys created, wrapped, and stored securely—even in unprotected NVM.</li>
<li><strong>On-Chip Enrollment: </strong>The chip generates its own root secret internally—no external key injection required, simplifying manufacturing and supply chain security.</li>
<li><strong>Secure Key Output: </strong>Controlled release of derived keys to other crypto modules via a dedicated hardware path.</li>
<li><strong>PUF Monitoring &amp; Built-In Self-Test (Logic BIST): </strong>Health monitoring and self-diagnostics for in-field reliability assurance.</li>
<li><strong>Hardware Context Inputs: </strong>Lifecycle management support for secure state transitions from manufacturing through end-of-life.</li>
<li><strong>Custom Hardware Personalization: </strong>Configurable personalization for application-specific requirements.</li>
<li><strong>Security Countermeasures: </strong>Advanced protections against side-channel attacks, fault injection, and reverse engineering.</li>
</ul>
<p>Synopsys Automotive PUF Premium is backed by a comprehensive set of safety and security deliverables that streamline integration and accelerate certification:</p>
<ul>
<li>ISO 26262 functional safety: Quality Manual, DFMEA, FMEDA, Safety Manual, DFA, Safety Case Report, ISO 26262 Assessment Report</li>
<li>ISO/SAE 21434 cybersecurity: Interface Report, Security Risk Analysis Report, Cybersecurity Case Report, Assessment Report, IP-SIRT services</li>
</ul>
<h2>Securing the full automotive lifecycle</h2>
<p>The value of a PUF-based root of trust extends across every stage of the automotive lifecycle. In manufacturing, the PUF eliminates the need to inject sensitive root keys from external systems—the chip generates its own unique secret internally, avoiding the complexity and cost of secure provisioning infrastructure.</p>
<p>In the field, the PUF enables strong device authentication for V2X communications, secure boot that verifies firmware integrity before execution, and encrypted data binding that ensures sensitive information is accessible only on the specific chip it was created for. For over-the-air (OTA) updates—now standard for connected vehicles—the PUF provides the cryptographic anchor ensuring updates are authentic and untampered.</p>
<h2>Battle-tested. Mission-ready.</h2>
<p>Automotive environments are unforgiving—but Synopsys SRAM PUF technology is built to withstand them. It has been extensively characterized from −40°C to 150°C, across voltage extremes, and over decades of accelerated silicon aging. Advanced algorithms for error correction, data de-biasing, and anti-aging keep PUF values rock-solid throughout the entire product lifecycle. The result is reliability backed by peer-reviewed research and validated in more than 1.5 billion deployed devices.</p>
<p>The Synopsys Automotive PUF meets the stringent functional safety and cybersecurity requirements in a single, certified IP. It is battle-tested, built on more than two decades of SRAM PUF research driven by recognized world-leading experts and over 15 years of deployment in aerospace and defense/government markets—environments where the margin for error is effectively zero. That same proven foundation extends naturally to adjacent mission-critical markets—from industrial robotics requiring functional safety to medical devices where patient safety depends on uncompromising device integrity (Figure 2).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279653" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?resize=1200%2C675&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1200" height="675" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?w=1200&amp;ssl=1 1200w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Synopsys_Automotive-Grade-PUF-IP-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Extending hardware root of trust across mission-critical markets.</strong></p>
<h2>Setting the bar for automotive silicon security</h2>
<p>As the automotive industry accelerates toward autonomous driving, electrification, and pervasive connectivity, the security and safety of every silicon component are non-negotiable. The Synopsys Automotive PUF Premium IP is the industry&#8217;s first PUF IP to deliver both ISO 26262/ASIL B functional safety and ISO/SAE 21434 cybersecurity compliance in a single, proven solution—backed by SRAM PUF technology deployed in over 1.5 billion devices and certified at the highest industry levels, including PSA Certified Level 3, SESIP Level 3, CC EAL6+, and FIPS 140-3 readiness.</p>
<p>For automotive SoC designers, this means a faster, lower-risk path to compliance—with a root of trust that integrates seamlessly across any foundry and process node, requires no per-technology tuning, and has been battle-tested across the most extreme operating conditions on the planet.</p>
<p>Learn more: Visit the <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/designware-ip/security-ip/cryptography-ip/puf/security-puf-ip.html">Synopsys PUF Premium web page</a> and download the <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/resources/puf-base-premium-datasheet.html">Synopsys PUF datasheet</a>.</p>

		<title>As Space Gets Connected, Security Gets Critical</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/as-space-gets-connected-security-gets-critical/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/as-space-gets-connected-security-gets-critical/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Liz Allan]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:03:08 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
